## 7️⃣ How the pieces fit together (the “big picture”)

| Layer | Responsibility | Key Code |
|-------|----------------|----------|
| **Configuration** | Centralised, environment‑driven settings (DB URL, bcrypt cost) | `config.py` |
| **Model** | Declarative table definition with a **unique e‑mail** constraint | `models.py` |
| **Utilities** | Password policy, bcrypt hashing & verification | `utils.py` |
| **Repository** | Transactional CRUD + authentication logic; handles **IntegrityError** for duplicate e‑mail | `repository.py` |
| **Application** | Orchestrates user‑registration & login flows (could be a Flask/Django view, CLI, etc.) | `app.py` |

*All database interactions are wrapped in a **session** that is **committed** only after successful validation, guaranteeing atomicity.*  
*The unique constraint is enforced by PostgreSQL, so even if two concurrent requests try to create the same e‑mail, one will receive an `IntegrityError`.*

---

## 8️⃣ Production hardening checklist

| ✅ Item | Why it matters |
|--------|----------------|
| **Use TLS/SSL** for DB connections (`postgresql+psycopg2://…?sslmode=require`) | Prevents password hashes from being sniffed on the wire. |
| **Rotate bcrypt cost** periodically (e.g., increase from 12 → 13) | Makes brute‑force harder as hardware improves. |
| **Rate‑limit login attempts** (e.g., via a reverse proxy or in‑app middleware) | Thwarts credential‑stuffing attacks. |
| **Account lockout / exponential back‑off** after N consecutive failures | Stops online password‑guessing. |
| **Store only the hash** (never the plain password) and **never log** it. |
| **Audit logs** for registration & authentication events (who, when, IP). |
| **Backup & point‑in‑time recovery** for the PostgreSQL cluster. |
| **Secrets management** – keep `DATABASE_URL` out of source control (env vars, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, …). |
| **Run migrations** (Alembic) instead of `create_all` for schema changes in real deployments. |
| **Static code analysis** – run `bandit` or `pylint` to catch insecure patterns. |

---

Below is a **step‑by‑step playbook** you can use to launch a sustainable‑focused product line, from idea generation to a market‑ready launch that leans on the latest eco‑trends and credible certifications.

---

## 1️⃣ Ideation – Sustainable Product Concepts

| # | Product Category | Core Eco‑Feature | Example Materials / Tech | Why It Resonates Today |
|---|------------------|------------------|--------------------------|------------------------|
| 1 | **Home & Kitchen** | Zero‑waste, reusable | Stainless‑steel straws, silicone food‑storage bags, compostable dishcloths (linen + bamboo) | Consumers are cutting single‑use plastics at home. |
| 2 | **Personal Care** | Biodegradable & refillable | Shampoo/conditioner bars, refill stations for body wash, bamboo toothbrushes with plant‑based bristles | “Plastic‑free bathroom” is a top search term. |
| 3 | **Apparel & Accessories** | Circular & low‑impact fibers | T‑shirts made from recycled polyester + organic cotton blend, shoes from up‑cycled ocean plastics, biodegradable sneakers (e.g., natural rubber sole) | Fast‑fashion backlash → demand for “closed‑loop” apparel. |
| 4 | **Office Supplies** | Recycled & carbon‑neutral | Recycled‑paper notebooks with FSC certification, plant‑based ink pens, biodegradable phone cases (PLA) | Remote‑work boom → greener home office setups. |
| 5 | **Outdoor & Travel** | Lightweight, renewable | Reusable water bottles from stainless steel + plant‑based coating, solar‑powered chargers, biodegradable travel kits (toothbrush, floss, soap) | Adventure‑travelers want gear that leaves no trace. |
| 6 | **Pet Products** | Compostable & responsibly sourced | Hemp dog leashes, biodegradable poop bags, recycled‑plastic pet toys | Pet‑owner market is growing 6% YoY and is highly brand‑loyal. |
| 7 | **Food & Beverage** | Up‑cycled ingredients | Snacks made from spent‑grain, fruit‑pomace protein powders, coffee made from “second‑grade” beans | Up‑cycling reduces food waste and adds a story hook. |
| 8 | **Kids & Baby** | Non‑toxic, renewable | Organic cotton onesies, bamboo baby blankets, plant‑based diaper liners | Parents prioritize safety & sustainability. |

> **Tip:** Start with **2–3 flagship items** that you can prototype quickly (e.g., a reusable water bottle + a biodegradable phone case). Use them as “anchor products” to build the rest of the line.

---

## 2️⃣ Target Market Segments

| Segment | Demographic / Psychographic | Key Pain Points | Buying Triggers |
|---------|----------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Eco‑Conscious Millennials** (25‑38) | Urban, higher education, values experiences over stuff | Distrust of green‑washing, wants proof | Transparent sourcing, certifications, storytelling |
| **Gen Z “Activist” Shoppers** (18‑24) | Social‑media native, values inclusivity & climate action | Wants to see impact, not just product | Influencer collaborations, user‑generated content, carbon‑offset badge |
| **Affluent Professionals** (30‑55) | High disposable income, seeks premium, low‑maintenance | Time‑starved, wants convenience | Luxury‑grade sustainable materials, sleek design, subscription refill service |
| **Corporate B2B (Gifts/Swag)** | HR & sustainability officers, ESG reporting | Need to meet ESG goals, avoid “green‑wash” accusations | Bulk certifications, custom branding, carbon‑neutral shipping |
| **Pet Owners** (30‑55) | Family‑oriented, willing to spend extra on pet health | Concerned about chemicals, waste | Natural, biodegradable, pet‑safe labeling |
| **Outdoor Enthusiasts** (25‑45) | Hikers, campers, “leave no trace” ethic | Need durable, lightweight gear | Rugged design, recycled content, repair‑ability program |

> **Prioritization:** If you’re a small‑to‑mid business, start with **Eco‑Conscious Millennials + Gen Z** (high social reach) and **Corporate B2B** (larger order size). Expand to niche segments later.

---

## 3️⃣ Marketing Strategy – “Eco‑Impact First”

### 3.1 Brand Positioning & Messaging
| Pillar | Core Message | Proof Point |
|--------|--------------|-------------|
| **Purpose‑Driven** | “Every product is a step toward a circular future.” | Life‑cycle assessment (LCA) showing X% carbon reduction vs. conventional alternatives. |
| **Transparency** | “See the journey from raw material to your hands.” | QR code on packaging linking to a live supply‑chain dashboard. |
| **Performance** | “Sustainable doesn’t mean compromise.” | Lab‑tested durability, performance metrics (e.g., 30% longer lifespan). |
| **Community** | “Join the zero‑waste movement.” | Membership program that tracks personal waste saved, offers rewards. |

### 3.2 Channels & Tactics
| Channel | Tactics | KPI |
|---------|---------|-----|
| **Social (IG, TikTok, Pinterest)** | Short‑form “behind‑the‑scenes” reels, product‑use hacks, influencer “day‑in‑the‑life” swaps | Engagement rate, follower growth, UGC volume |
| **Content Hub (Blog/SEO)** | Guides: “How to build a zero‑waste kitchen,” “Carbon‑footprint calculator” | Organic traffic, time‑on‑page, lead capture |
| **Email + Automation** | Welcome series with sustainability education, product‑care tips, refill reminders | Open rate, conversion rate, repeat purchase |
| **PR & Partnerships** | Pitch to eco‑focused media (e.g., TreeHugger, EcoWatch), co‑brand with NGOs (e.g., 1% for the Planet) | Earned media mentions, referral traffic |
| **Retail/Pop‑up** | Sustainable‑themed pop‑ups in eco‑markets, “try‑before‑you‑buy” stations | Foot traffic, on‑site sales |
| **B2B Sales** | Dedicated ESG sales deck, bulk‑order discounts, custom branding | Number of corporate accounts, average order value |

### 3.3 Storytelling Assets
- **Impact Dashboard** (online): Shows total plastic saved, CO₂ avoided, trees planted.
- **Packaging QR Code**: Scans to a micro‑video of the material’s origin.
- **Customer “Eco‑Hero” Spotlights**: Feature users who achieve measurable waste reduction.

---

## 4️⃣ Aligning with Current Sustainability Trends & Certifications

| Trend | How to Leverage | Recommended Certifications |
|-------|----------------|----------------------------|
| **Circular Economy** (reuse, repair, recycle) | Offer product‑take‑back & refurbish program; design for disassembly | **Cradle‑to‑Cradle (C2C)**, **B Corp** |
| **Carbon Neutrality** | Conduct LCA, offset remaining emissions via verified projects | **Carbon Trust Standard**, **Climate Neutral Certified** |
| **Regenerative Materials** (e.g., hemp, mycelium) | Use hemp fibers for textiles, mycelium foam for packaging | **Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS)** for organic fibers |
| **Plastic‑Free Packaging** | Use compostable PLA, recycled cardboard, plant‑based inks | **Compostable Certification (BPI)**, **FSC** for paper |
| **Transparency & Traceability** | Blockchain or QR‑code traceability of raw material origins | **Fair Trade Certified**, **USDA Organic** (if applicable) |
| **Social Impact** | Pay fair wages, support community projects | **Fair Trade**, **B Corp** |
| **Zero‑Waste Design** | Design products that can be fully recycled or composted at end‑of‑life | **Zero Waste International Alliance** (ZWI) guidelines |

> **Fast‑Track Tip:** For a first launch, aim for **2–3 core certifications** (e.g., **FSC** for packaging, **Carbon Trust** for carbon neutrality, and **B Corp** for overall impact). These are widely recognized and can be obtained within 3–6 months with a focused audit.

---

## 5️⃣ Product Development Roadmap (6‑Month Sprint)

| Week | Milestone | Deliverable |
|------|-----------|-------------|
| 1‑2 | **Market Validation** | Survey 200‑300 target users → top 3 product concepts |
| 3‑4 | **Concept Prototyping** | Sketches, material samples, cost sheet |
| 5‑6 | **Supplier Vetting** | Identify 2‑3 vetted sustainable suppliers, request eco‑data sheets |
| 7‑8 | **Life‑Cycle Assessment (LCA)** | Draft LCA for each prototype (use open‑source tools like **OpenLCA**) |
| 9‑10 | **Certification Scoping** | Contact certifying bodies, gather documentation requirements |
| 11‑12 | **Design Finalization** | CAD files, packaging mock‑ups with QR‑code integration |
| 13‑14 | **Pilot Production** | Small batch (100‑200 units) for testing |
| 15‑16 | **User Testing & Feedback** | Collect durability, usability, and perception data |
| 17‑18 | **Iterate & Scale** | Refine design, finalize supply contracts |
| 19‑20 | **Certification Submission** | Submit for chosen certifications |
| 21‑22 | **Marketing Asset Build** | Photo/video shoots, impact dashboard, launch copy |
| 23‑24 | **Soft Launch** | Limited release to email list + influencer seeding |
| 25‑26 | **Full Launch** | E‑commerce site live, B2B outreach, PR push |
| Ongoing | **Metrics & Optimization** | Track carbon saved, repeat purchase, NPS; iterate quarterly |

---

## 6️⃣ Success Metrics (KPIs)

| Category | Metric | Target (12 mo) |
|----------|--------|----------------|
| **Environmental Impact** | CO₂e avoided (kg) | ≥ 10 t |
| | Plastic waste diverted (kg) | ≥ 5 t |
| **Financial** | Gross revenue | 1.5× initial forecast |
| | Repeat purchase rate | ≥ 30 % |
| **Brand** | Net Promoter Score (NPS) | ≥ 70 |
| | Earned media mentions | 30+ high‑authority outlets |
| **Certification** | Certifications obtained | 3 core (FSC, Carbon Trust, B Corp) |
| **Community** | # of Eco‑Hero stories shared | 100+ user‑generated posts |

---

## 7️⃣ Quick‑Start Checklist

1. **Pick 2‑3 flagship products** (e.g., reusable bottle + biodegradable phone case).  
2. **Validate demand** with a short survey or social‑media poll.  
3. **Source sustainable materials** – request environmental data sheets.  
4. **Run a rapid LCA** (free tools: OpenLCA, SimaPro trial).  
5. **Select certifications** that align with your product (FSC, Carbon Trust, B Corp).  
6. **Create a visual brand story** (mission, impact dashboard, QR‑code).  
7. **Build a launch funnel** – teaser content → email capture → pre‑order.  
8. **Partner with an influencer** who has a proven eco‑audience (micro‑influencers 10‑50 k often have higher engagement).  
9. **Set up a take‑back/reuse program** from day 1 (even a simple mail‑in recycling box).  
10. **Track and publish impact** monthly to keep the community engaged.

---

### 🎯 Bottom Line

- **Start small, think big:** A focused, high‑impact product line (2‑3 items) lets you perfect the sustainability story, secure certifications, and prove the model before scaling.
- **Proof over promise:** Transparent data (LCA, QR‑code traceability) and reputable certifications are the strongest antidotes to green‑washing skepticism.
- **Community is your catalyst:** Turn customers into “Eco‑Heroes” who share their waste‑reduction numbers; this fuels organic growth and builds brand loyalty.

seekatweet-1:
**Short answer:**  
Use the **Twitter API v2 “Followers” endpoint**:

```
GET https://api.twitter.com/2/users/:id/followers
```

(Replace `:id` with the numeric user‑ID you already have.)

If you’re still on the older v1.1 API, the equivalent calls are:

* `GET https://api.twitter.com/1.1/followers/ids.json?user_id=12345` – returns only user IDs.  
* `GET https://api.twitter.com/1.1/followers/list.json?user_id=12345` – returns full user objects (up to 20 per request).

Both require OAuth 1.0a user‑auth (or OAuth 2.0 Bearer token for v2) and are subject to the standard rate limits (15 requests per 15 min for v1.1, 900 requests per 15 min for v2).

---

### How to call the v2 endpoint

| Parameter | Required? | Description |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| `max_results` | No | Number of results per page (default 100, max 1000). |
| `pagination_token` | No | Token returned in the previous response for pagination. |
| `user.fields` | No | Comma‑separated list of extra fields you want (e.g., `username,created_at`). |
| `expansions` | No | Expand related objects (e.g., `pinned_tweet_id`). |

**Example (cURL)**

```bash
curl -X GET "https://api.twitter.com/2/users/2244994945/followers?max_results=1000&user.fields=username,created_at" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_BEARER_TOKEN"
```

The response looks like:

```json
{
  "data": [
    { "id": "123", "name": "Alice", "username": "alice" },
    { "id": "456", "name": "Bob",   "username": "bob"   }
    // …
  ],
  "meta": {
    "result_count": 1000,
    "next_token": "b26v89c19zqg8o3fpd3..."
  }
}
```

If `next_token` is present, keep calling the endpoint with `pagination_token=next_token` until it disappears – that’s how you walk through the entire follower list.

---

### When to use the v1.1 endpoints

* **`followers/ids`** – If you only need the numeric IDs (cheaper on rate‑limit budget). Returns up to 5 000 IDs per request; paginate with `cursor`.
* **`followers/list`** – If you need the full user objects (screen name, profile image, etc.) but only a small batch (max 20 per request). Also paginated with `cursor`.

**Example (cURL, v1.1)**

```bash
curl -X GET "https://api.twitter.com/1.1/followers/ids.json?user_id=2244994945&count=5000&cursor=-1" \
     -H "Authorization: OAuth oauth_consumer_key=\"...\", oauth_token=\"...\", ..."
```

---

### Quick checklist

1. **Choose the API version** you’re comfortable with (v2 is recommended for new projects).  
2. **Obtain the proper credentials** – Bearer token for v2, OAuth 1.0a user token for v1.1.  
3. **Make the request** using the endpoint above.  
4. **Handle pagination** (`next_token` for v2, `cursor` for v1.1) until you’ve retrieved all followers.  
5. **Respect rate limits** – pause or back‑off when you hit the limit.

---

**Relevant tags:** `twitter-api`, `followers`, `endpoint`, `rest-api`, `pagination`, `oauth`.

showhear-1:
**Solution Explanation**

For a sequence  

```
a1 , a2 , … , aN          ( 1 ≤ N ≤ 10^6 )
```

we have to choose a non‑empty contiguous part (a *subarray*)

```
ai , ai+1 , … , aj          ( 1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ N )
```

whose sum is as large as possible.  
The answer is the value

```
max{  Σk=i..j ak  |  1 ≤ i ≤ j ≤ N } .
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1.  Kadane’s algorithm  

While scanning the array from left to right we keep two numbers

* `cur` – the maximum sum of a subarray that **ends** at the current
  position.
* `best` – the maximum sum of any subarray seen so far.

When we read a new element `x`

```
cur = max( x , cur + x )
```

* either we start a new subarray consisting only of `x`,
* or we extend the previous best‑ending‑here subarray by `x`.

Then we update the global answer

```
best = max( best , cur )
```

Initially both `cur` and `best` are set to the first element,
so the algorithm works even when all numbers are negative
(the answer will be the largest (least negative) element).

The scan needs only constant extra memory and touches each element once,
hence runs in **O(N)** time.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.  Correctness Proof  

We prove that the algorithm outputs the maximum possible subarray sum.

---

##### Lemma 1  
After processing the first `k` elements (`k ≥ 1`), `cur` equals the
maximum sum of a subarray that ends at position `k`.

**Proof.**  
Induction over `k`.

*Base (`k = 1`).*  
`cur` is initialised with `a1`, which is the only subarray ending at 1,
so the statement holds.

*Induction step.*  
Assume the statement true after element `k‑1`.  
When element `ak` is read we set  

```
cur' = max( ak , cur + ak )
```

* `ak` corresponds to the subarray consisting of the single element `ak`,
  which indeed ends at `k`.
* `cur + ak` corresponds to the best subarray ending at `k‑1`
  (induction hypothesis) extended by `ak`; this also ends at `k`.

No other subarray can end at `k`, therefore `cur'` is exactly the
maximum sum of a subarray ending at `k`. ∎



##### Lemma 2  
After processing the first `k` elements, `best` equals the maximum sum of
**any** subarray completely contained in the prefix `a1 … ak`.

**Proof.**  
Induction over `k`.

*Base (`k = 1`).*  
`best = a1`, the only subarray of the prefix, so the claim holds.

*Induction step.*  
Assume the claim true after element `k‑1`.  
When `ak` is processed we first compute the correct `cur` (Lemma 1)
and then set  

```
best' = max( best , cur )
```

* `best` is the optimum among subarrays that lie completely inside the
  first `k‑1` positions (induction hypothesis).
* `cur` is the optimum among subarrays that **must** end at position `k`
  (Lemma 1).

Every subarray of the first `k` elements either ends at `k` or lies
entirely in the first `k‑1` positions, therefore `best'` is the optimum
for the whole prefix. ∎



##### Lemma 3  
When the scan finishes (`k = N`), `best` equals the maximum sum of a
subarray of the whole array.

**Proof.**  
Directly from Lemma 2 with `k = N`. ∎



##### Theorem  
The algorithm outputs the maximum possible sum of a non‑empty subarray.

**Proof.**  
At termination the algorithm prints `best`. By Lemma 3 this value is
exactly the optimum required by the problem statement. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 3.  Complexity Analysis  

*Time* – each of the `N` numbers is read and processed once: **O(N)**.  
*Memory* – only a few 64‑bit variables are stored: **O(1)**.

The sum of up to `10^6` numbers of absolute value `10^6` fits into
`int64` (`|sum| ≤ 10^12`), so `long long` is sufficient.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 4.  Reference Implementation  (C++17)

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    
    int N;
    if (!(cin >> N)) return 0;
    long long x;
    cin >> x;                     // first element
    long long cur = x, best = x;  // initialise

    for (int i = 1; i < N; ++i) {
        cin >> x;
        cur = max(x, cur + x);    // best subarray ending here
        best = max(best, cur);    // best overall so far
    }

    cout << best << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

The program follows exactly the algorithm proven correct above and
conforms to the GNU++17 compiler.

musotik-1:
**Solution Explanation**

For every square `i` ( `1 ≤ i ≤ N` ) the token may be moved to a square `j`

* `j > i`   (to the right)
* `A[j] > A[i]` (to a larger value)

If a player cannot move, he loses.  
Both players play perfectly, Alice moves first.  
For every test case we have to decide whether the starting position
(square `1`) is winning for the first player.



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1.   Game as an impartial game

The board together with the allowed moves is a **directed acyclic graph**
(only edges to the right, therefore no cycles).

For a position `i`

```
G(i) = mex { G(j) | j > i  and  A[j] > A[i] }          (1)
```

`G(i)` – Grundy number of square `i` – is the smallest non‑negative
integer that is **not** contained in the set on the right side.
The start position is winning **iff** `G(1) ≠ 0`.

So we only have to compute `G(1)`.



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.   What is needed for a mex query ?

While we are processing the squares from right to left,
all squares with index larger than the current one are already known.
For a fixed Grundy number `g` we store

```
maxVal[g] = maximum A[j] among already processed squares with G(j)=g
```

If for the current square `i` we have `maxVal[g] > A[i]`,
there exists a reachable square with Grundy `g`,
otherwise there is none.

Therefore

```
G(i) = smallest g with  maxVal[g] ≤ A[i]                (2)
```

After `G(i)` is known we insert the pair `(A[i] , G(i))`
into the structure, i.e. we set

```
maxVal[ G(i) ] = max( maxVal[ G(i) ] , A[i] )           (3)
```

Now the problem is reduced to a data structure that supports

* **point update** – increase `maxVal[g]`
* **range query** – given `x = A[i]` find the smallest `g`
  with `maxVal[g] ≤ x`

Both operations have to be fast.



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 3.   Segment tree over Grundy numbers

`G(i)` can never be larger than `N` (mex of at most `N` different
numbers), therefore we build a segment tree for the indices  

```
g = 0 , 1 , … , N                (N+1 leaves)
```

*leaf `g`* stores `maxVal[g]`.  
*inner node* stores the **maximum** of its children.
Initially every `maxVal[g] = 0` (no square processed yet,
`A[i] ≥ 1`).

* **update** – point update of leaf `g` with value `A[i]`
  (store the larger of the old and the new value).  
  `O(log N)`

* **mex query** – we need the first leaf whose stored value is
  `≤ x`.  
  Starting at the root (range `[L,R]`)

```
if left child's maximum ≤ x   → answer is inside the left child
else                           → answer is inside the right child
```

  The walk goes down one level each step, therefore `O(log N)`.



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 4.   Whole algorithm for one test case

```
read N and array A[1…N]
build a segment tree of size N+1, all leaves = 0

for i = N … 1                     // right to left
        g = mexQuery( A[i] )      // smallest g with maxVal[g] ≤ A[i]
        if i == 1   grundyStart = g
        pointUpdate( g , A[i] )   // maxVal[g] = max(…, A[i])

answer = (grundyStart != 0) ? "YES" : "NO"
```

`mexQuery` and `pointUpdate` are the two segment‑tree operations described
above.

*Time complexity* per test case  

```
N queries  +  N updates   →   O(N log N)
```

*Memory consumption*  

```
array A          : O(N)
segment tree     : 4·(N+1) integers  →  O(N)
```

Both satisfy the limits (`Σ N ≤ 10⁶`).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 5.   Correctness Proof  

We prove that the algorithm prints “YES” exactly for the test cases
where Alice (the first player) has a winning strategy.

---

##### Lemma 1  
While processing the squares from right to left,
just before the iteration for index `i` the segment tree contains,
for every Grundy number `g`,
the maximum value among **all** squares `j` with `j > i` and `G(j)=g`.

**Proof.**  
Induction over the loop.

*Base.* Before the first iteration (`i = N`) no square has been
processed, all leaves store `0`.  
`0` is indeed the maximum value among an empty set.

*Induction step.* Assume the statement true before handling square `i`.
The algorithm computes `g = G(i)` using the current tree,
then updates leaf `g` with `A[i]`.  
Consequently after the update the leaf `g` stores the maximum of the
previous value (maximum among squares `j > i`) and `A[i]`,
i.e. the maximum among squares `j ≥ i`.  
All other leaves stay unchanged, therefore the invariant holds for the
next iteration (`i‑1`). ∎



##### Lemma 2  
For a fixed square `i` let  

```
S(i) = { G(j) | j > i  and  A[j] > A[i] } .
```

The value returned by `mexQuery(A[i])` equals `mex( S(i) )`.

**Proof.**  
By Lemma 1, for every Grundy number `g`

```
maxVal[g] > A[i]   ⇔   there exists a square j>i with G(j)=g and A[j] > A[i]
```

Hence the set `{ g | maxVal[g] > A[i] }` is exactly `S(i)`.  
`mexQuery` returns the smallest `g` with `maxVal[g] ≤ A[i]`,
i.e. the smallest non‑negative integer **not** belonging to `S(i)`,
which is the definition of `mex( S(i) )`. ∎



##### Lemma 3  
The algorithm stores in `grundyStart` the Grundy number `G(1)` of the
initial position.

**Proof.**  
During the loop the iteration with `i = 1` computes `g = mexQuery(A[1])`.
By Lemma 2 this `g` equals `mex( S(1) )`, which is exactly the
definition (1) of `G(1)`.  
The algorithm saves this value into `grundyStart`. ∎



##### Lemma 4  
If `grundyStart = 0` then the starting position is losing for the
player to move; otherwise it is winning.

**Proof.**  
The game is impartial and the graph of moves is acyclic,
therefore the Sprague‑Grundy theory applies.
A position is losing **iff** its Grundy number is `0`,
winning otherwise. ∎



##### Theorem  
For every test case the algorithm outputs  

*“YES”*  **iff** Alice has a winning strategy.

**Proof.**  

*If part.*  
Algorithm prints “YES” only when `grundyStart ≠ 0`.
By Lemma 3 `grundyStart = G(1)`.  
By Lemma 4 a non‑zero Grundy number means the start position is
winning for the player to move, i.e. Alice can force a win.

*Only‑if part.*  
Assume Alice can force a win.
Then the start position is winning, consequently its Grundy number is
non‑zero (Lemma 4).  
By Lemma 3 the algorithm stores this non‑zero number in
`grundyStart` and prints “YES”. ∎



##### Corollary  
The program prints “YES” exactly for the test cases where Alice wins,
and “NO” otherwise. ∎



--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 6.   Reference Implementation  (C++17)

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

/* segment tree that stores for each Grundy number g the maximal A
   among already processed squares with Grundy g                */
struct SegTree {
    int n;                     // number of leaves = max Grundy + 1
    vector<int> t;             // maximum on the interval

    SegTree(int _n = 0) { init(_n); }

    void init(int _n) {
        n = _n;
        t.assign(4 * n, 0);    // all leaves = 0  (no square processed yet)
    }

    // point update: leaf pos gets max(old, val)
    void update(int pos, int val, int v, int l, int r) {
        if (l == r) {
            t[v] = max(t[v], val);
            return;
        }
        int m = (l + r) >> 1;
        if (pos <= m) update(pos, val, v << 1, l, m);
        else          update(pos, val, v << 1 | 1, m + 1, r);
        t[v] = max(t[v << 1], t[v << 1 | 1]);
    }
    void update(int pos, int val) { update(pos, val, 1, 0, n - 1); }

    // mex query: smallest index g with t[leaf g] ≤ x
    int mex(int x, int v, int l, int r) const {
        if (l == r) return l;
        int m = (l + r) >> 1;
        if (t[v << 1] <= x) return mex(x, v << 1, l, m);
        else                return mex(x, v << 1 | 1, m + 1, r);
    }
    int mex(int x) const { return mex(x, 1, 0, n - 1); }
};

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);
    int T;
    if (!(cin >> T)) return 0;
    while (T--) {
        int N;
        cin >> N;
        vector<int> A(N + 1);
        for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) cin >> A[i];

        // Grundy numbers are in [0 .. N]
        SegTree seg(N + 1);               // leaves 0 … N
        int grundyStart = 0;              // will become G(1)

        for (int i = N; i >= 1; --i) {
            int g = seg.mex(A[i]);        // Lemma 2
            if (i == 1) grundyStart = g; // Lemma 3
            seg.update(g, A[i]);          // Lemma 1 (3)
        }

        cout << (grundyStart != 0 ? "YES" : "NO") << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

The program follows exactly the algorithm proven correct above and
conforms to the GNU++17 compiler.

google-apps-and-box.net-1:
Below is a concise, step‑by‑step playbook for getting **real‑time, in‑place editing of Google Workspace docs from inside Box** – and having every change land back in Box automatically.

---

## 1️⃣ The “gold‑standard” integration: **Box for Google Workspace** (formerly *Box for G Suite*)

| What it does | Why it matters |
|--------------|----------------|
| **Open‑with** button in the Box UI that launches a Google Doc, Sheet, or Slide directly from Box. | Users never have to download → upload; they stay in the same workflow. |
| **Save to Box** button (or automatic “Box” icon) inside the Google editor. | Every edit is persisted back to the original Box file – no manual re‑upload. |
| **Single‑sign‑on (SSO) & permission sync** (Box permissions are honoured in Google Workspace). | No extra sharing steps; security stays consistent. |
| **Activity logging** in Box (who edited, when, what changed). | Auditable trail for compliance teams. |
| **Collaboration** – multiple users can edit simultaneously, just like native Google files. | Teams keep the same real‑time co‑authoring experience. |

> **Bottom line:** This native integration is built, supported, and kept up‑to‑date by both Box and Google. It’s the fastest way to meet your “edit‑in‑place & auto‑save” requirement without custom code.

---

## 2️⃣ How to enable it (admin‑level + end‑user steps)

### A. Admin side – Box Admin Console
1. **Log in** to the Box Admin Console → **Apps** → **Custom Apps** → **Create Custom App**.  
   - Choose **OAuth 2.0 (User Auth)**.  
   - Name it *Box for Google Workspace* (or any friendly name).  
2. **Add the Google Workspace scopes** you need:  
   - `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.file` (read/write to the specific file)  
   - `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/documents` (Docs)  
   - `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/spreadsheets` (Sheets)  
   - `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/presentations` (Slides)  
3. **Save** → copy the **Client ID** and **Client Secret** – you’ll need them when you install the add‑on in Google Workspace.  
4. (Optional) **Enforce SSO**: under **Enterprise Settings → Single Sign‑On**, map Box groups to Google groups so that Box permissions automatically flow into Google.

### B. Admin side – Google Workspace Marketplace
1. Open the **Google Workspace Marketplace** → search for **Box for Google Workspace**.  
2. Click **Install** → **Domain install** (so every user in the org gets it).  
3. When prompted, **paste the Box Client ID & Secret** you copied earlier.  
4. Grant the requested OAuth scopes (the same ones you added in Box).  

> **Tip:** If you have a “Zero‑Trust” policy, enable **OAuth token verification** in both Box and Google to make sure tokens can’t be hijacked.

### C. End‑user workflow (what the user actually clicks)

| Step | Action | What you see |
|------|--------|--------------|
| 1️⃣ | In Box (web, mobile, or Box Drive) locate a `.docx`, `.xlsx`, or `.pptx` file. | File thumbnail with a **Google Docs** (or Sheets/Slides) icon appears. |
| 2️⃣ | Click **Open with → Google Docs** (or Sheets/Slides). | The file opens in a new browser tab **as a native Google file**. |
| 3️⃣ | Edit the document as usual (real‑time co‑authoring, comments, etc.). | No “download → upload” steps. |
| 4️⃣ | When you’re done, click the **Box icon** in the Google editor toolbar (or **File → Save to Box**). | The editor automatically pushes the latest version back to the original Box file. |
| 5️⃣ | Return to Box – you’ll see a **new version** (Box version history) with a timestamp and your name. | Auditable change log is created automatically. |

> **Result:** The file lives **only** in Box, but you get the full Google editing experience. Every save creates a new Box version, so you can roll back at any time.

---

## 3️⃣ Alternative (if you need a fallback or extra flexibility)

| Option | When to use it | How it works |
|--------|----------------|--------------|
| **Box Drive + Google Drive “Open with”** | Small teams that already rely heavily on Google Drive and want a local‑file feel. | Box Drive syncs the Box folder to a local drive. From the synced folder you open the file → Google Docs (web) → changes are saved back to Box because the file’s *origin* is still Box. |
| **Box Relay (Workflow Automation)** | You want to trigger extra actions (e.g., convert to PDF, notify a Slack channel) **after** a Google edit is saved. | Create a Relay workflow: *When a new version is added to Box → Convert → Email → Archive*. |
| **Custom API integration (Box API + Google Docs API)** | Very specific UI/UX requirements (e.g., embed a Google editor inside a custom intranet portal). | Use Box’s **Content API** to fetch the file, generate a **Google Docs “edit” URL** (`https://docs.google.com/document/d/<fileId>/edit?usp=box_edit`), and use the **Google Docs “Save to Box”** endpoint (`POST https://www.googleapis.com/drive/v3/files/<fileId>/copy`). |
| **Third‑party connectors (Zapier, Power Automate, Workato)** | You want to automate *non‑editing* actions (e.g., “When a Google Sheet is updated → copy to a specific Box folder”). | Simple “trigger → action” recipes; no code required. |

> **Recommendation:** Start with the native **Box for Google Workspace** add‑on. Only consider the custom API route if you have a truly unique UI requirement that the native integration can’t satisfy.

---

## 4️⃣ Best‑practice checklist (so the integration stays smooth over time)

| ✅ Checklist Item | ✅ How to verify |
|-------------------|-----------------|
| **Single source of truth** – keep the master file *only* in Box. | In Box, confirm the file type is *not* also stored in Google Drive. |
| **Versioning enabled** – Box must retain every edit as a new version. | Admin Console → **Content Settings → Versioning** set to “Keep all versions”. |
| **Permission parity** – Box folder permissions map to Google sharing. | Test with a user in a Box group that has *Viewer* rights → they should see *View‑only* in Google Docs. |
| **SSO / MFA enforced** on both platforms. | Attempt a login from a device that doesn’t have MFA – it should be blocked. |
| **Audit logs** – Box Activity Log shows “Edited with Google Docs”. | Admin Console → **Reports → Activity** → filter on *Open with Google Docs*. |
| **Token lifecycle** – set token expiration (Box: 60 days, Google: 1 hour refresh). | In Box → **Enterprise Settings → OAuth 2.0** → “Access token expiration”. |
| **User training** – short 5‑minute video or in‑app tip. | Record a quick “Open with → Save to Box” demo and pin it to the Box folder description. |
| **Support contract** – ensure both Box and Google support are covered. | Verify that the integration is listed under *Supported Integrations* in your Box Enterprise plan. |

---

## 4️⃣ Quick‑start cheat sheet (copy‑paste ready)

```text
# Box Admin Console
1. Apps → Custom Apps → New OAuth App
2. Scopes: drive.file, documents, spreadsheets, presentations
3. Save → copy Client ID / Secret

# Google Workspace Marketplace
1. Install “Box for Google Workspace” (domain install)
2. Paste Box Client ID & Secret
3. Accept OAuth scopes

# User workflow
1. In Box → Open with → Google Docs/Sheets/Slides
2. Edit in Google editor
3. Click Box icon (or File → Save to Box)
4. Return to Box → see new version
```

---

### TL;DR

**Enable the native “Box for Google Workspace” add‑on** (admin‑install both sides, grant the proper OAuth scopes, and let users use the **Open with → Google Docs** button in Box). The editor’s **Save to Box** action automatically creates a new version in Box, giving you exactly the “edit‑directly‑from‑Box & auto‑save back to Box” experience with zero manual file juggling.  

If you ever need extra automation (notifications, PDF conversion, etc.), layer **Box Relay** or a simple **Zapier/Power Automate** flow on top of the same integration – but the core editing requirement is fully satisfied out‑of‑the‑box.

In the middle of the city’s endless grid, where the traffic lights blinked like nervous fireflies, Lina found a crack in the wall of an abandoned bakery. It was a thin seam of brick, half‑covered by a graffiti tag of a bluebird, and when she brushed the paint away a faint scent of jasmine rose, as if the air itself had been waiting.

She slipped through the opening and entered a courtyard that did not belong to any map. The cobblestones were smooth, worn by generations that never existed in the city’s records. Ivy curled around a rusted wrought‑iron gate, and a single magnolia tree stood in the center, its blossoms opening and closing in a rhythm that matched the distant hum of the subway.

The garden was ordinary enough to be believed: a bench, a stone fountain that whispered water even though its basin was dry, and a row of lavender that swayed without wind. Yet every time Lina sat on the bench, the city’s clamor faded to a muffled echo, and the sky above the magnolia shifted from the familiar steel‑gray to a deep, liquid indigo speckled with unfamiliar constellations.

She began to visit each evening after work, bringing a notebook to sketch the strange flora that seemed to rearrange themselves while she was not looking. One night, a silver moth landed on the magnolia’s trunk and, without moving its wings, traced a delicate spiral in the air. The spiral lingered, a faint glow that pulsed like a heartbeat. When Lina reached out, her fingertips brushed the light and felt a cool current, as if a river ran beneath the garden’s surface.

The next morning, the city’s newspaper reported a sudden surge of rain in a district that had been dry for weeks. Lina looked at the magnolia and saw a single droplet hanging from a petal, reflecting a landscape she could not name—a valley of amber light and towering arches of stone. The droplet fell, and the garden’s stone fountain filled with water that did not belong to any pipe.

Lina never told anyone about the garden. She kept the secret in the same way she kept the city’s secrets: by walking past them, pretending they were just part of the scenery. Yet when she passed the bakery’s cracked wall, she could hear, faint as a sigh, the magnolia’s leaves rustle in a language that sounded like an invitation. And sometimes, on nights when the city lights dimmed, she felt the garden’s pull, a gentle tug at the edge of her thoughts, reminding her that some doors open not with a push, but with a quiet, knowing step.

**The Case of the Vanishing Violin**

Detective Mara Larkin was known throughout the city for two things: her uncanny ability to read people and the strange, humming pocket watch she always wore. The watch was a family heirloom, its brass case etched with a spiral of tiny symbols that no one could decipher—except Mara. She had spent years learning the subtle ticks and pauses of its inner gears, turning it into a personal metronome for intuition.

When the famed Stradivarius violin of Maestro Antonelli disappeared from the grand concert hall the night before its debut, the police were baffled. The security system showed no breach, the glass case was intact, and the only clue was a faint, lingering scent of sandalwood in the empty display.

Mara arrived at the hall, her watch ticking softly against her wrist. She closed her eyes, inhaled the cool air, and let the watch’s rhythm guide her thoughts. The watch’s second hand moved in a pattern she’d learned to associate with “hidden layers”—a slow, deliberate sweep followed by a rapid flicker. It was a signal that the answer lay beneath the surface, not in the obvious.

She began by examining the hall’s acoustics. The concert hall was designed to amplify sound, but Mara knew that every note also carried a fingerprint of the space it traveled through. She placed a small, portable recorder near the empty case and played a recording of the violin’s last rehearsal. As the notes filled the room, she listened for any irregularities.

The watch’s ticking quickened. Mara’s ears caught a faint echo—a soft, metallic resonance that didn’t belong to the violin’s timbre. It was the sound of a string being plucked, but not from a violin. She followed the echo to a concealed ventilation shaft behind the stage curtains.

Inside the shaft, she found a narrow tunnel lined with old, forgotten props. At the far end, a small wooden crate rested on a platform. The crate was sealed with a simple latch, but the scent of sandalwood was stronger here. Mara lifted the latch, and the crate opened to reveal the missing Stradivarius, nestled in a bed of velvet.

A single note lay on top of the violin: a handwritten slip that read, “For the love of music, I needed a new home.”

Mara’s watch ticked a final, steady beat. She understood the unique method that had led her to the truth: she had used the watch not as a timepiece, but as a conduit for her own intuition, translating its rhythm into a sensory map of the environment. By listening to the subtle “beats” of the world—smell, sound, vibration—she uncovered the hidden layer where the thief had concealed the priceless instrument.

The thief turned out to be the hall’s own chief stagehand, a former violinist who had been denied a chance to play on a Stradivarius. He had hidden the instrument in the ventilation shaft, hoping to retrieve it later when the hall was empty.

Mara returned the violin to Maestro Antonelli, who performed the debut as planned, the notes soaring higher than ever. As the audience applauded, Mara slipped her watch back onto her wrist, its brass case catching the stage lights. The watch ticked on, a reminder that sometimes the most powerful detective work isn’t about following clues on paper, but about listening to the hidden rhythms that surround us.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Trap errors and report line number
trap 'echo "Error: command failed at line $LINENO."' ERR

# Configuration
PROJECT_DIR="myproject"
VENV_DIR="venv"
MAIN_FILE="main.py"
REQUIRED_PKG="requests"

# Helper functions
error_exit() {
    echo "Fatal: $1" >&2
    exit 1
}

find_python() {
    if command -v python3.8 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        echo "python3.8"
        return
    fi
    if command -v python3 >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        local ver
        ver=$(python3 -c 'import sys; print("{}.{}".format(sys.version_info[0], sys.version_info[1]))')
        if [[ "$ver" == "3.8" ]]; then
            echo "python3"
            return
        fi
    fi
    error_exit "Python 3.8 interpreter not found."
}

# Verify external commands
command -v git >/dev/null 2>&1 || error_exit "git is not installed."

PYTHON_BIN=$(find_python)

# Create project directory if missing
if [[ ! -d "$PROJECT_DIR" ]]; then
    mkdir -p "$PROJECT_DIR"
    echo "Created directory '$PROJECT_DIR'."
fi

cd "$PROJECT_DIR"

# Initialise git repository if needed
if [[ ! -d ".git" ]]; then
    git init
    echo "Initialized new Git repository."
fi

# Add a basic .gitignore if absent
if [[ ! -f ".gitignore" ]]; then
    cat > .gitignore <<'EOF'
venv/
__pycache__/
*.pyc
EOF
    echo "Added .gitignore."
fi

# Set up virtual environment
if [[ ! -d "$VENV_DIR" ]]; then
    "$PYTHON_BIN" -m venv "$VENV_DIR"
    echo "Virtual environment created in '$VENV_DIR'."
fi

# Activate virtual environment
# shellcheck source=/dev/null
source "$VENV_DIR/bin/activate"

# Upgrade pip quietly
pip install --quiet --upgrade pip

# Install required package if not already present
if ! pip show "$REQUIRED_PKG" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    pip install --quiet "$REQUIRED_PKG"
    echo "Installed $REQUIRED_PKG."
else
    echo "$REQUIRED_PKG already installed."
fi

# Create main.py with expected content if missing or different
if [[ ! -f "$MAIN_FILE" ]] || ! grep -Fxq 'print("Hello, World!")' "$MAIN_FILE"; then
    cat > "$MAIN_FILE" <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
print("Hello, World!")
EOF
    chmod +x "$MAIN_FILE"
    echo "Created $MAIN_FILE."
else
    echo "$MAIN_FILE already contains the expected code."
fi

# Stage and commit any changes if there are uncommitted modifications
if [[ -n "$(git status --porcelain)" ]]; then
    git add -A
    git commit -m "Initial project setup"
    echo "Committed initial files to Git."
else
    echo "No changes to commit."
fi

echo "Project setup complete."
exit 0
```

**The Neon Kitchen**

*Beginning*  
In the humming sprawl of Nova‑Arc, glass towers rose like crystal ribs, their façades flickering with holo‑ads for synthetic meals and instant nutrition pods. Below, the old market district clung to its cobblestones, where steam‑bent lanterns still cast amber light over stalls of fermented kelp and hand‑rolled spice ribbons. Arin, a twenty‑something courier who zipped between the sky‑trams and the market’s alleys, had never cared for food beyond the nutrient packs his employer supplied. He loved the rush of data streams, the click of his wrist‑pad as he delivered encrypted parcels, but the scent of simmering broth never reached him.

One rain‑slick night, a delivery went awry. A cracked holo‑crate slipped from his grip, spilling a cascade of glowing, nanotech-infused ingredients onto the market’s central square. The nanobots sparked, forming a shimmering lattice that hovered above the puddles. A curious old vendor, Mei, who still cooked over a coal fire, laughed and said, “Even the future can’t hide a good recipe.” She beckoned Arin to help clean the mess, and as he knelt, the nanobots swirled around his fingertips, reacting to his pulse.

*Middle*  
The moment his skin brushed the glowing particles, a rush of flavors erupted in his mind—sweetness of solar‑citrus, the umami of algae harvested from the orbital farms, the smoky depth of ancient wood‑fire. Instinctively, he began to stir, his hands moving as if guided by a forgotten rhythm. The nanobots obeyed, arranging the ingredients into a perfect broth that hissed and sang. Mei watched, eyes widening. “You have the taste of the old world and the code of the new,” she whispered.

Word spread fast. In a city where AI chefs could print meals in seconds, a human with a hidden culinary talent was a novelty. Arin was invited to the annual Fusion Festival, where holographic judges evaluated dishes on both sensory impact and algorithmic precision. He spent days in Mei’s cramped kitchen, learning the stories behind each spice, while his wrist‑pad logged the nanobot patterns, translating them into a digital symphony of taste.

When the night of the festival arrived, Arin stood before a crowd of neon‑clad spectators and floating drones. He poured the broth into a translucent bowl, letting the nanobots cascade like liquid light. The aroma rose, weaving the scent of rain‑kissed streets with the distant hum of the sky‑trams. The judges tasted, their sensors flashing green, then their faces softened as the flavors resonated with memories of home and hope.

*End*  
Arin’s dish won the Grand Synthesis award, not because it was the most technologically advanced, but because it honored the city’s dual heartbeat—its relentless progress and its stubborn traditions. He realized his hidden talent was not a secret to keep, but a bridge between worlds. From that night on, he split his time between courier routes and the neon kitchen, teaching others that even in a future of instant meals, the soul of cooking still lived in the hands of those willing to listen to the whisper of spices and the pulse of nanobots alike.

In the city’s endless hum, Mara slipped between laundry lines and the clatter of tram rails, chasing a silver‑spotted cat that seemed to know every cracked sidewalk. The cat darted into a narrow alley where the brick wall was half‑overgrown with ivy, its leaves forming a faint, green‑tinted doorway. No one else ever paused there; the street vendors shouted, the bus horns blared, and the cat slipped through as if the world had forgotten the passage.

Mara pushed the rusted gate, and it sighed open with a sound like a sigh of old paper. Inside, the air was cooler, scented with jasmine that bloomed despite the December chill. A stone fountain at the center poured water that glowed faintly, reflecting not the sky but the faces of people who had once sat on the moss‑soft benches—each ripple a memory of laughter, a whispered secret, a lost love. The city’s noise was muffled, as if the garden were a lung exhaling a softer breath.

A woman in a faded apron tended the beds, her hands moving with a rhythm that matched the city’s heartbeat. She did not look surprised when Mara entered; she simply nodded, as if greeting a neighbor who had always been there. “The garden remembers,” she said, handing Mara a single rose that opened in her palm, its petals turning a shade of the girl’s own childhood home.

The rose’s scent carried a faint murmur—names of those who had walked the garden before, spoken in a language of wind and rustle. Mara heard her own name among them, and the garden seemed to smile, its vines curling a little tighter around the gate, as if to keep the secret safe.

Mara visited each day after school, slipping through the gate with the cat at her heels. She learned that the garden’s water showed not only reflections but also the moments people chose to forget, and the bench beneath the oak remembered the weight of every story told upon it. In the city’s relentless rush, the garden existed as an ordinary pocket of green, its subtle magic woven into the fabric of daily life—accepted, unremarkable, and yet, for Mara, a place where the impossible grew as naturally as the weeds on the sidewalk.

Think of the list as a “menu” you can pick from – you don’t have to implement every item, only the ones that match your product requirements.

---

## 1️⃣ Authentication & Authorization
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect** | Third‑party login (Google, Facebook, Apple) and token‑based identity. |
| **JWT (JSON Web Token) issuance & validation** | Stateless session tokens for API calls. |
| **Refresh‑Token endpoint** | Rotate access tokens without re‑authenticating. |
| **MFA / TOTP endpoint** | Optional two‑factor authentication. |
| **Password‑reset & email‑verification flows** | Secure account recovery. |

---

## 2️⃣ User & Profile Management
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Create / Update / Delete User** | Register, edit profile, deactivate. |
| **Get User Profile** | Public view of a user’s basic info (username, avatar, bio). |
| **Upload / Delete Avatar** | Media upload endpoint (often re‑used with the Media API). |
| **Follow / Unfollow** | Manage “friend” / “follow” relationships. |
| **Block / Report User** | Moderation‑related user actions. |
| **Privacy Settings** | Toggle visibility of email, posts, etc. |

---

## 3️⃣ Content (Posts) Management
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Create Post** | Text + optional media IDs, tags, location. |
| **Edit / Delete Post** | Update or remove a post. |
| **Get Post (single)** | Retrieve a post with its metadata. |
| **List Posts (feed)** | Paginated feed for a user or a public timeline. |
| **Search Posts** | Full‑text / hashtag search. |
| **Pin / Feature Post** | Highlight a post on a profile. |

---

## 4️⃣ Media Handling
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Initiate Multipart Upload** | Get pre‑signed URLs (S3, GCS, Azure) for large files. |
| **Complete Upload** | Finalize the media object, trigger processing. |
| **Media Processing webhook** | Notify when transcoding, thumbnail generation, or virus‑scan finishes. |
| **Get Media URL** | Return CDN‑optimized, signed URL for playback/download. |
| **Delete Media** | Remove media and associated thumbnails. |
| **Streaming / Adaptive bitrate endpoint** | HLS/DASH manifest delivery for video. |

---

## 5️⃣ Social Interactions (Comments, Likes, Reactions)
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Add Comment** | Attach a comment to a post (or reply to another comment). |
| **Edit / Delete Comment** | Manage own comments. |
| **List Comments** | Paginated comment thread, with sorting (newest/most‑liked). |
| **Add Reaction / Like** | Record a like or any custom reaction (emoji). |
| **Remove Reaction** | Undo a like/reaction. |
| **Get Reaction Summary** | Count of each reaction type per post/comment. |

---

## 6️⃣ Notification System
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Create Notification** | Internal service that writes a notification record (e.g., “X liked your post”). |
| **List Notifications** | Pull‑based inbox (paginated, unread count). |
| **Mark as Read / Delete** | Manage notification state. |
| **Push Notification endpoint** | Send device‑specific push (APNs, FCM) payloads. |
| **WebSocket / Server‑Sent Events (SSE) stream** | Real‑time push of in‑app notifications. |
| **Email / SMS notification webhook** | Optional out‑of‑band alerts. |

---

## 7️⃣ Real‑Time Updates & Messaging
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **WebSocket connection handshake** | Upgrade HTTP to WS for live feed updates. |
| **Subscribe / Unsubscribe topics** | Choose which event streams (new posts, comments, likes) to receive. |
| **Publish Event** | Internal service that pushes events to the WS/SSE broker. |
| **Direct Messaging (optional)** | Send/receive private messages (CRUD + read receipts). |
| **Presence / Typing indicators** | Small payloads for online status. |

---

## 8️⃣ Search & Discovery
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Full‑text / Elasticsearch query** | Search posts, users, hashtags. |
| **Autocomplete / Trending tags** | Suggest popular terms as the user types. |
| **Explore / Recommended Content** | Return curated or algorithmic suggestions. |
| **Geo‑search** | Find posts near a location. |

---

## 9️⃣ Moderation & Safety
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Report Content** | Flag a post/comment/media for review. |
| **Content Review Queue** | List items awaiting moderator action. |
| **Take Action (remove, hide, warn)** | Moderator tools to enforce policy. |
| **Automated Toxicity / Image‑moderation webhook** | Integration with ML services (Perspective API, AWS Rekognition, etc.). |
| **User‑level sanctions** | Suspend / ban user, revoke tokens. |

---

## 🔟 Analytics & Metrics
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Track Event** | Log page view, click, share, etc. (client‑side SDK or server endpoint). |
| **Get User‑level Stats** | Number of followers, total likes, post count. |
| **Aggregate Dashboard endpoints** | Daily active users, retention, engagement rates. |
| **A/B‑test variant fetch** | Return experiment bucket for the client. |
| **Export / Data‑warehouse connector** | Push raw events to BigQuery, Redshift, Snowflake. |

---

## 1️⃣1️⃣ Billing / Payments (if you monetize)
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Create Subscription / Purchase** | Connect to Stripe/PayPal for premium features. |
| **Validate Receipt** | Verify in‑app purchase tokens. |
| **Get Billing History** | List past invoices, receipts. |
| **Upgrade / Downgrade Plan** | Change subscription tier. |

---

## 1️⃣2️⃣ System & Infrastructure
| API | What it does |
|-----|--------------|
| **Health‑check endpoint** | `/health` for load balancers / monitoring. |
| **Version / Feature‑flag endpoint** | `/meta` returns API version, enabled features. |
| **Rate‑limit status** | Return remaining quota (`X-RateLimit-Remaining`). |
| **Audit‑log endpoint** | Secure read‑only view of critical actions (admin only). |
| **Webhooks management** | Register external URLs for events (e.g., “post_created”). |

---

### How to Use This List
1. **Pick the categories** that match your product scope (most social apps need 1‑7, plus 8‑10 for a polished experience).  
2. **Define the contract** (HTTP method, request/response schema, auth scopes) for each API.  
3. **Group related endpoints** into micro‑services or modules (e.g., `auth-service`, `post-service`, `media-service`).  
4. **Add versioning** (`/v1/users`, `/v2/posts`) so you can evolve the API without breaking clients.  

Feel free to extend or trim the list – it’s a starter “menu” that covers the typical functional surface of a modern social‑media platform. Happy building! 🚀

social-mirror-1:
**Short answer**

```bash
find /path/to/dir -type f -print
```

That one‑liner prints the full pathname of **every regular file** under `/path/to/dir`, recursing into all sub‑directories.

---

## Why `find`?

`find` is the classic Unix tool for walking a directory tree.  
It:

* Traverses *all* sub‑directories (no depth limit unless you ask for one).  
* Lets you filter by type (`-type f` for regular files), name, size, timestamps, permissions, etc.  
* Can format the output (`-printf`, `-ls`) or hand each file to another command (`-exec`, `-execdir`, `xargs`).  

Because it does the traversal itself, you don’t need to combine `ls`, `grep`, `awk`, etc.; a single `find` does the job reliably even when filenames contain spaces, newlines, or other “funny” characters.

---

## The basic command

```bash
find /path/to/dir -type f -print
```

* `/path/to/dir` – the directory you want to start from. Use `.` for “the current directory”.
* `-type f` – restricts results to **regular files** (excludes directories, symlinks, device nodes, sockets, etc.).
* `-print` – the default action; prints each file’s full pathname, one per line.

**Example**

```bash
$ cd /etc
$ find . -type f -print | head -n 5
./passwd
./group
./hosts
./hostname
./hosts.allow
```

---

## Common variations & useful options

| Goal | Command | Explanation |
|------|---------|-------------|
| **Only files, no directories** | `find . -type f` | `-print` is implicit. |
| **Show file size and modification time** | `find . -type f -ls` | `-ls` prints a long `ls -dils`‑style line for each file. |
| **Custom output format** | `find . -type f -printf '%p %s bytes %TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS\n'` | `%p` = path, `%s` = size, `%TY…%TS` = timestamp. |
| **Limit depth** (e.g., only the top two levels) | `find . -maxdepth 2 -type f` | `-maxdepth N` stops descending after N levels. |
| **Skip a particular subtree** | `find . -path './skipme*' -prune -o -type f -print` | `-prune` tells `find` not to descend into matching paths. |
| **Find files matching a pattern** | `find . -type f -name '*.conf'` | `-name` uses shell‑style globbing (case‑sensitive). |
| **Case‑insensitive name match** | `find . -type f -iname '*.conf'` | `-iname` ignores case. |
| **Find empty files** | `find . -type f -empty` | `-empty` matches zero‑length regular files (or empty directories if `-type d`). |
| ** Oculus‑style “list only the names” (no leading `./`)** | `find . -type f -printf '%f\n'` | `%f` prints just the filename (basename). |
| **Pipe to another command safely** (e.g., `md5sum`) | `find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 md5sum` | `-print0` separates names with NUL, safe for any characters. |
| **Run a command on each file** | `find . -type f -exec chmod u+rw {} \;` | `-exec … {} \;` runs the command once per file. |
| **Run a command on batches of files** | `find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 rm -f` | `xargs` builds larger argument lists, reducing process overhead. |
| **Exclude hidden files** (those whose name starts with `.`) | `find . -type f ! -name '.*'` | `!` negates the test. |
| **List only files newer than 7 days** | `find . -type f -mtime -7` | `-mtime n` matches files modified *n* days ago; `-7` = less than 7 days. |
| **List only files larger than 10 MiB** | `find . -type f -size +10M` | `+10M` = greater than 10 MiB. |
| **Follow symbolic links** | `find -L . -type f` | `-L` tells `find` to follow symlinks (otherwise it treats them as files themselves). |
| **Suppress error messages** (e.g., permission denied) | `find . -type f 2>/dev/null` | Redirect `stderr` to `/dev/null`. |

---

## Handling “weird” filenames

If you need to feed the list to another command, **never** rely on plain whitespace‑separated output. Use the NUL‑terminated forms:

```bash
# Safe for any filename (including newlines, spaces, tabs, etc.)
find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 <command>
```

or the `-exec` form, which runs the command directly on each file:

```bash
find . -type f -exec <command> {} \;
```

Both approaches avoid the classic “filename with spaces breaks the pipeline” problem.

---

## A few concrete use‑cases

### 1. Dump the list to a file (for later processing)

```bash
find /var/log -type f > /tmp/all-log-files.txt
```

Now `/tmp/all-log-files.txt` contains one absolute (or relative) pathname per line.

### 2. Count how many files there are

```bash
find . -type f | wc -l
```

### 3. Compute total size of all files

```bash
find . -type f -printf '%s\n' | awk '{total+=$1} END {print total}'
```

or, using `du` on the same list:

```bash
find . -type f -print0 | du --files0-from=- -ch | tail -1
```

### 4. Generate a “tree‑like” listing without using `tree`

```bash
find . -type f -printf '%p\n' | sed -e 's|[^/]*/|│   |g' -e 's|│   \([^│]\)|├── \1|'
```

(That’s a quick‑and‑dirty visual, but `find` is the engine behind it.)

### 5. Remove *all* files (dangerous – use with care!)

```bash
find . -type f -delete
```

`-delete` is built‑in to `find` and is safer than `rm -rf *` because it only removes files, not directories, and it respects the traversal order.

---

## When `find` isn’t enough (or you want a prettier view)

* **`tree`** – prints a nice indented tree, optionally with file sizes (`tree -a -s`).  
* **`ls -R`** – recursive `ls`, but its output is not as easy to filter and can break on weird filenames.  
* **`fd`** (a modern, faster alternative to `find`) – e.g., `fd -t f` does the same thing with a nicer syntax.

Nevertheless, for scripting, portability, and fine‑grained filtering, `find` remains the go‑to tool.

---

## TL;DR cheat‑sheet

```bash
# 1. All regular files, full paths
find . -type f

# 2. Same, but only two levels deep
find . -maxdepth 2 -type f

# 3. Only *.txt files, case‑insensitive
find . -type f -iname '*.txt'

# 4. Print path + size (bytes) + mtime
find . -type f -printf '%p %s %TY-%Tm-%Td %TH:%TM:%TS\n'

# 5. Hand each file to another command (e.g., md5sum)
find . -type f -print0 | xargs -0 md5sum

# 6. Exclude a directory named "tmp"
find . -path './tmp*' -prune -o -type f -print
```

All of the above are just variations on the same core idea: **`find <start‑dir> -type f …`**. Adjust the tests (`-name`, `-size`, `-mtime`, `-prune`, `-maxdepth`, etc.) to suit whatever subset of files you need.

The rain hammered the city’s sidewalks, turning the streets into a blur of silver and gray. Daniel had spent the last ten years shuffling between construction sites, his hands calloused from steel and concrete, his evenings filled with the low hum of traffic and the occasional clink of a bottle in a cheap bar. Music was something he heard on the radio while driving home, a background to his life rather than a part of it.

One Saturday, after a particularly grueling week, he decided to take a shortcut through an old, abandoned warehouse on the edge of town. The building was a relic of a different era—its wooden beams still sturdy, its windows boarded up, and in the far corner, half hidden beneath a dusty tarp, stood a grand piano. Its mahogany case was scarred, the ivory keys yellowed with age, but the instrument still held an undeniable presence.

Curiosity tugged at him. He lifted the tarp, revealing the piano’s polished surface, and brushed his fingers over the keys. A faint, resonant note rang out, startling him. He laughed at himself, feeling foolish, but something inside him urged him to press another key. The sound that followed was richer, fuller, as if the piano itself were sighing in relief after years of silence.

He sat down on the cracked wooden bench, his knees trembling. The first chord he struck was clumsy, a hesitant mixture of major and minor, but as his fingers found their places, a melody began to emerge—simple at first, then growing in complexity. The notes flowed effortlessly, as if they had been waiting for his hands to discover them. He was surprised by the ease with which his fingers moved, the way his body seemed to anticipate each progression.

Hours slipped by unnoticed. The rain outside turned to a gentle drizzle, then stopped altogether. When he finally rose, his palms were sore, but his heart was light. He realized that the piano had unlocked something he never knew existed—a hidden talent that had lain dormant, waiting for the right moment to surface.

Word spread quickly among the few people who still passed by the warehouse. A local music teacher, intrigued by the rumors, visited the next day. She watched Daniel play, her eyes widening with each phrase. “You have a natural gift,” she said, smiling. “You just needed a chance to hear it.”

From that day forward, Daniel split his time between the construction sites and the piano. He took lessons, practiced late into the night, and eventually performed at a small community hall, his music echoing through the room like a secret finally revealed. The man who once measured his life in concrete and steel now measured it in chords and harmonies, grateful for the hidden talent that had turned a rainy shortcut into a lifelong symphony.

Below is a **step‑by‑step checklist** you can follow to get a domain name, web hosting, a live website, and a professional‑looking email address up and running.  
After the checklist you’ll find a short list of **clarifying questions** that will help me tailor the recommendations to your exact needs (budget, technical comfort, type of site, etc.).

---

## 1️⃣ Choose & Register a Domain Name  

| Step | What to Do | Why It Matters |
|------|------------|----------------|
| **1.1 Brainstorm** | Write down a few short, memorable, brand‑relevant names. Aim for `.com` if possible; otherwise consider `.net`, `.org`, or a relevant TLD (`.shop`, `.tech`, etc.). | A good domain is easy to type, spell, and remember. |
| **1.2 Check Availability** | Use a registrar’s search tool (e.g., Namecheap, Google Domains, GoDaddy). | Guarantees you can actually own the name. |
| **1.3 Register** | Purchase the domain for at least 1 year (most registrars let you lock it for 5‑10 years). Enable **privacy protection** (WHOIS‑guard) if you don’t want your personal contact info public. | Secures ownership and protects your personal data. |
| **1.4 Note the DNS provider** | Most registrars double as DNS hosts, but you can point the domain to a third‑party DNS service (Cloudflare, Amazon Route 53) later if you need advanced features. | DNS is how the domain finds your web server and email servers. |

**Typical Costs** – $10‑$20 / year for a standard `.com`. Premium names or specialty TLDs can be more expensive.

---

## 2️⃣ Pick a Web Hosting Solution  

| Hosting Type | Best For | Typical Price (per month) | Example Providers |
|--------------|----------|---------------------------|-------------------|
| **Shared Hosting** | Small blogs, brochure sites, low traffic | $3‑$10 | SiteGround, Bluehost, A2 Hosting |
| **Managed WordPress** | WordPress sites, want automatic updates & backups | $10‑$30 | WP Engine, Kinsta, Flywheel |
| **VPS / Cloud VM** | Medium traffic, need more control (root access) | $20‑$80 | DigitalOcean, Linode, Vultr |
| **Managed Cloud (e.g., AWS Lightsail, Google Cloud Run)** | Developers who want scalability without deep sysadmin work | $5‑$30 | Lightsail, Google App Engine |
| **Website Builder (Wix, Squarespace, Shopify)** | No‑code, drag‑and‑drop, e‑commerce | $12‑$40 | Wix, Squarespace, Shopify |

**What to look for**  

1. **SSL/TLS support** (most hosts provide a free Let’s Encrypt cert).  
2. **One‑click installs** for popular CMSs (WordPress, Joomla, etc.).  
3. **Backup & restore** options.  
4. **Customer support** (24/7 chat is a plus).  

---

## 3️⃣ Connect Domain → Hosting (DNS Configuration)

1. **Find your host’s nameservers** (e.g., `ns1.hostprovider.com`, `ns2.hostprovider.com`).  
2. **Log into your domain registrar** → DNS settings → replace the default nameservers with the host’s nameservers.  
   *If you prefer to keep the registrar’s DNS:* add an **A record** pointing `@` (the root) to your server’s IP address, and a **CNAME** for `www` → `@`.  
3. **Propagation** – DNS changes usually propagate within minutes to a few hours. Use `dig`, `nslookup`, or online tools like “whatsmydns.net” to verify.

---

## 4️⃣ Install & Configure Your Website  

### 4.1 Choose a Platform  
| Platform | Use‑Case | Learning Curve |
|----------|----------|----------------|
| **WordPress** | Blogs, business sites, e‑commerce (via WooCommerce) | Low‑medium (lots of tutorials) |
| **Static Site Generators** (Hugo, Jekyll, Eleventy) | Fast, low‑maintenance sites, developers | Medium‑high (requires build step) |
| **Shopify / BigCommerce** | Full‑featured online stores | Low (hosted solution) |
| **Custom code (HTML/CSS/JS)** | One‑page landing pages, portfolios | Low (if you already have code) |

### 4.2 One‑Click Install (most shared hosts)  
- Log into your hosting control panel (cPanel, Plesk, or custom dashboard).  
- Look for “Softaculous”, “Installatron”, or “One‑Click Apps”.  
- Choose **WordPress**, fill in site title, admin user/password, and click **Install**.  

### 4.3 Manual Install (if needed)  
1. **Upload files** via FTP/SFTP or the host’s file manager.  
2. **Create a MySQL database** and user.  
3. **Run the installer** (e.g., `wp-admin/install.php`).  

### 4.4 Secure the Site  
- **Enable HTTPS** (most hosts auto‑install Let’s Encrypt; otherwise request a cert).  
- **Update** core, themes, plugins regularly.  
- **Install a security plugin** (Wordfence, Sucuri) if using WordPress.  

---

## 5️⃣ Set Up a Professional Email Address  

You have three main routes:

| Option | How It Works | Pros | Cons | Typical Cost |
|--------|--------------|------|------|--------------|
| **Email via Hosting** | Use the host’s mail server (e.g., `mail.yourdomain.com`). Create accounts in cPanel → Email Accounts. | Free (included with most plans). | Often limited storage, poorer spam filtering, may get blocked by some receivers. | $0 (included) |
| **Google Workspace (formerly G Suite)** | Cloud‑based Gmail for your domain (`you@yourdomain.com`). | Excellent spam protection, 30 GB+ storage, collaboration tools (Docs, Drive). | $6‑$18 / user / month. | $6‑$18 |
| **Microsoft 365 Business** | Outlook/Exchange for your domain. | Strong Office integration, 50 GB mailbox, Teams. | $5‑$12 / user / month. | $5‑$12 |
| **Third‑Party Email‑Only Services** (Zoho Mail, ProtonMail, FastMail) | Dedicated email hosting, often with a free tier for a few users. | Good privacy, simple UI. | Limited features on free plans. | $0‑$5 |

### 5.1 Quick Setup with Google Workspace (example)

1. **Sign up** at workspace.google.com → “Get Started”.  
2. **Verify domain ownership** – Google will give you a TXT record to add to your DNS (same place you edited for the website).  
3. **Create user accounts** (`you@yourdomain.com`).  
4. **Update MX records** – Google provides a set of MX entries (e.g., `ASPMX.L.GOOGLE.COM`). Replace any existing MX records with these.  
5. **Wait for DNS propagation** (usually < 30 min).  
6. **Log in** to Gmail with your new address; you can also configure Outlook, Apple Mail, or mobile clients using the standard IMAP/SMTP settings Google provides.

### 5.2 If You Use Hosting‑Provided Email

1. In cPanel → **Email Accounts** → “Create”.  
2. Choose a strong password, set mailbox quota.  
3. **Set MX record** – often the host automatically creates an MX pointing to `mail.yourdomain.com`. Verify it in your DNS zone.  
4. **Configure a mail client** (Thunderbird, Outlook, iPhone Mail) using the host’s IMAP/SMTP settings (usually listed in the hosting help docs).  

---

## 6️⃣ Test Everything Before Going Live  

| Test | How |
|------|-----|
| **Website reachable** | Open `http://yourdomain.com` and `https://yourdomain.com` in multiple browsers. |
| **SSL/TLS** | Use SSL Labs’ test (`https://www.ssllabs.com/ssltest/`) to confirm the cert is trusted and no mixed‑content warnings. |
| **Email sending/receiving** | Send a test email to a personal address (Gmail, Outlook) and reply. Check spam folder. |
| **Form submissions** (if any) | Submit a contact form, verify you receive the email. |
| **Performance** | Run a quick PageSpeed Insights test; aim for < 2 s load time. |
| **Backup** | Ensure your host’s backup feature is enabled or set up a manual backup schedule. |

---

## 7️⃣ Ongoing Maintenance  

1. **Update** CMS, plugins, themes at least monthly.  
2. **Renew** domain and hosting before expiration (set auto‑renew if possible).  
3. **Monitor** site uptime (UptimeRobot, Pingdom) and email deliverability (Mail‑tester.com).  
4. **Backup** – keep at least one off‑site copy (e.g., to Google Drive, Dropbox, or an external server).  

---

# 📋 Clarifying Questions (to fine‑tune the advice)

1. **What type of website are you building?**  
   - Simple brochure/landing page?  
   - Blog or news site?  
   - E‑commerce store?  
   - Portfolio or custom web app?  

2. **Do you have a preferred platform or technology?**

3. **Estimated traffic / resource needs?**

4. **Budget constraints?**

5. **Technical comfort level?**

6. **Do you need multiple email addresses or just one?**  
   - If you need a team mailbox, a Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 plan may be more cost‑effective.  

7. **Any specific compliance or privacy requirements?**  
   - GDPR, HIPAA, etc., that might affect where you host or which email provider you choose.  

8. **Do you already have a domain or hosting provider you’d like to keep?**  

9. **Do you need a custom SSL certificate (EV, wildcard) or is a free Let’s Encrypt cert fine?**  

---

**Next steps:**  
- Answer the questions above (or just let me know which parts you already have decided on).

## 1️⃣ Which API is the “best” for a one‑off 100 k‑character translation?

| Goal | Recommended free API |
|------|----------------------|
| **Highest translation quality (EN↔DE/FR/ES/IT/JA)** | **DeepL Free** – 500 k char/month, 5 k per request. |

> **Bottom line:** If you can split the text into ≤ 5 k‑char chunks, **Microsoft Translator** or **DeepL** give you the most generous free quotas and the best quality. If you prefer a single request, **IBM Watson Lite** (50 k limit) or a self‑hosted **LibreTranslate** instance are the way to go.

---

## 2️⃣ How to split a 100 k‑character string safely

Most services impose a **character‑count limit** *and* a **sentence‑boundary recommendation** (to avoid cutting a sentence in half). A simple, language‑agnostic splitter:

```python
import re, textwrap

def chunk_text(text, max_len=5000):
    # Split on sentence boundaries first (period, ?, !, newline)
    sentences = re.split(r'(?<=[.!?])\s+', text)
    chunks = []
    cur = ''
    for s in sentences:
        if len(cur) + len(s) + 1 <= max_len:
            cur = (cur + ' ' + s).strip()
        else:
            chunks.append(cur)
            cur = s
    if cur:
        chunks.append(cur)
    return chunks
```

- **Result:** a list of ≤ `max_len`‑character pieces that respect sentence boundaries.
- **Tip:** For languages without clear punctuation (e.g., Chinese), split on a fixed character count.

- **Rate limit:** ~5 req / sec per key; you can add a short `time.sleep(0.2)` between calls if you hit 429.  
- **Supported languages:** 70+ (see Azure docs).

---

### B. LibreTranslate (self‑hosted Docker)

If you don’t want any cloud‑account, spin up a container locally:

```bash
docker run -d -p 5000:5000 libretranslate/libretranslate
```

Now the API is reachable at `http://localhost:5000`.

```python
import requests

def libre_translate(text, source="en", target="fr"):
    url = "http://localhost:5000/translate"
    payload = {
        "q": text,
        "source": source,
        "target": target,
        "format": "text"
    }
    r = requests.post(url, json=payload)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["translatedText"]

def translate_document_libre(text, source="en", target="fr", max_len=5000):
    chunks = chunk_text(text, max_len)
    return " ".join(libre_translate(c, source, target) for c in chunks)

# Example
if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open("big_input.txt", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        src = f.read()
    print(translate_document_libre(src, source="en", target="de")[:500])
```

**Why LibreTranslate?**

- **Unlimited** (only limited by your hardware).  
- **No API key** (optional token for public instances).  
- **Open‑source** – you can replace the underlying MarianMT model with a larger one (e.g., Helsinki‑NLP) if you need higher quality.

## 4️⃣ Practical tips for a smooth experience

| Issue | Fix / Best practice |
|-------|----------------------|
| **Rate‑limit (429)** | Add exponential back‑off (`time.sleep(1)`, then 2 s, 4 s…) or respect the documented QPS (e.g., Azure 5 req/s). |
| **Character‑limit exceeded** | Always chunk **before** sending; never rely on the API to truncate. |
| **Unexpected language detection** | Explicitly set `source` language (most APIs accept `source=auto` but it can mis‑detect on short fragments). |
| **Cost creep** | Monitor usage via the provider’s dashboard; set alerts when you approach the free quota. |
| **Caching** | Store a hash of the source text → translation result (e.g., SQLite, Redis). This avoids re‑translating identical paragraphs. |
| **Batching** | Some services (e.g., Azure) allow sending **multiple** `Text` objects in a single POST (up to 100 items). This reduces HTTP overhead. |
| **Unicode handling** | Ensure you send UTF‑8 (`Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`). Most APIs accept it automatically. |
| **Legal / TOS** | Free tiers are usually for **development / low‑volume** use. If you plan to ship a commercial product, consider moving to a paid plan or self‑hosted solution. |

| **You need > 2 M char/month on a regular basis** | Consider a **paid plan** or **self‑hosted**; free tiers will run out quickly. |
